messages.author: 648d79fada138931
messages.subject: Standardizing covariates and polynomial terms in occupancy models
parts:
Hi! 
I'd greatly appreciate help with some issues I'm running into while performing occupancy modeling for the first time (with unmarked). 

Challenge+Question 1: 
Some of my occupancy predictor covariates have strong right skews, and I think this is the reason that univariate analysis of these covariates fail to converge (NaN values for beta coefficient SE/ p-values). Is the solution to center or standardize these covariates? Or some other data transformation?  Should I transform every occupancy covariate in my model or just the select few that are skewed? 

Challenge + Question 2: 
I'm trying to include polynomial terms for some occupancy covariates. When I run univariate analysis (including main effect + quadratic term) of the covariates, the beta coefficients and SE values are huge/abnormal (eg. Estimates >>10, SE >> 10).  When I remove the polynomial term, the coefficients/SE return to normal values.

 I show two examples of this issue below. In the first example, the covariate is also highly skewed to the right, so I applied the scale() function as well (although I am not sure if this is appropriate). For the second example, the covariate was not skewed so I did not scale. Does someone know what is going on here and how to deal with A) quadratic terms that produce extremely large coefficients/SE and B) quadratic terms where the covariate is also highly skewed? 

Example 1: 

Input: 
occu_distanceperm <- occu(formula = ~1~ scale(Distance_Perm) + I(scale(Distance_Perm^2)),data = occuframe_hosts, linkPsi = "logit" )

Output:
                                                         Estimate           SE            P(>|z| )
Intercept                                         4.099                3.4          0.229
scale(Distance_Perm)                  -3.29                 3.667     0.368
I(scale(Distance_Perm^2))          11.35                10.97      0.29 


Example 2: 
Input: 
occu_Phosphate <- occu(formula = ~ambient_temp + water_depth + weather ~ Phosphate + I(Phosphate^2), data = occuframe_hosts, linkPsi = "logit" )

Output: 
                                                         Estimate           SE            P(>|z| )
Intercept                                          6.321                5.5          0.251
Phosphate                                      -29.344              26.86     0.274
I(Phosphate^2)                              33.60               30.60       0.272 


Thank you so much,
Olivia

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Standardizing covariates and polynomial terms in occupancy models
parts:
Dear Olivia,

can you give a brief summary of your data set (number of sites, number of reps, observed proportion of sites with presence) ?

Stab at 1: For numerical reasons scaling continuous covariates so that their values are 'somewhat close to zero' is always helpful . However, there is a cost in the interpretation of the model, which becomes more challenging. So I only scale when I have to. When you have raw values of covs that are more extreme than, say, 5 or 10, then I'd scale. Note 1: I prefer scalings that help interpretation. For instance, a Julian date covariate I'd center and then divide by 30 rather than by the SD. This leads to units of 1 month, which I find helpful. Note 2: remember that we never scale factor levels.

Stab at 2: don't know, could be that your model is too complex when you add another term (the quadratic). See my question at the start.

Best regards – Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Standardizing covariates and polynomial terms in occupancy models
parts:
Hi Marc,

Thank you so much for your first thoughts. 

A brief summary of the dataset: I have 91 sites, 3 replicates at each site, and 42.8% naive occupancy of sites. I'm performing single species occupancy of lymnaeid snail hosts of Fascioloides magna. I collected a lot of occupancy covariates (10, 14 if including quadratic terms) and detection covariates (5, 7 if including quadratic terms), which has presented issues with model selection. These covariates all have some logical hypothesis/ a priori reasoning for exploring, so it is difficult to cut down. I decided to first perform univariate analysis to potentially limit the starting number of covariates for model selection procedures.  

A third question, when scaling quadratic terms, should you scale first (not within model) and then square? Or is the format I used correct?

All the best,
Olivia

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Standardizing covariates and polynomial terms in occupancy models
parts:
Dear Olivia,

OK, so you have some data and observed occupancy is not like 98% or something. Having said this, 10 occupancy covariates with 91 sites is asking a lot and means you have fewer than 10 "site data points" per parameter. I'd probably try to toss out any covariate that is not absolutely necessary, scale everything and use initial values from simpler models for more complex models.

Re. your third question: I think it doesn't matter and both orders of scaling/squaring should lead to the same predictions of occupancy vs. covariate (though to be sure I'd try it out).

Best regards  --- Marc
